detail: A re-run of 'worktree_orchestrate.py resolve' after a PARTIALLY COMPLETED resolve targets the wrong branch and attempts to delete main, locally and on the remote. Only git's own refusals prevented it. Exact sequence, observed: (1) resolve --commit began; 'git worktree remove --force' deletes the worktree's .git file early, then spends minutes rm-ing that worktree's .cache (19 GB of iOS derived data here) and exceeded the caller's 2-minute timeout, leaving the worktree dir present but its .git gone and git marking it 'prunable'. (2) resolve --commit re-run on the SAME --worktree path: with <worktree>/.git absent it cannot resolve that path to its branch and falls back to the CURRENT branch of the invoking cwd, which for the primary checkout is main. It printed '(x) no active registry record for branch=main' — it had a signal that its target was wrong — and proceeded to the destructive steps regardless. (3) executed: 'git worktree remove --force <path>' rc=128 ('.git does not exist'); 'git branch -D main' refused ONLY because main was checked out in the primary worktree; 'git push origin --delete main' refused ONLY because main is GitHub's default branch. Both refusals are external safety nets, not this tool's. If the repo's default branch were named something else (say prod), the push would have DELETED origin/main. If main had not been checked out, the local delete would have succeeded.
resolution: Three independent fixes, any one of which blocks the incident; do all three. (a) resolve must derive the branch from the worktree path via 'git worktree list --porcelain' and REFUSE when the path is absent, prunable, or maps to no branch — never fall back to the cwd's HEAD. (b) refuse outright when the resolved branch is the repo's base/default branch or is checked out in the primary worktree; deleting main is never a legitimate resolve outcome, so it should be unrepresentable rather than merely refused downstream. (c) treat 'no active registry record for branch=X' as a hard stop before any mutation, not a printed warning — the tool already detected the anomaly and continued. Separately: make teardown resilient to slow removals (the 19 GB .cache rm is what created the partial state) — remove .git LAST, or prune-then-rm so an interrupted run is re-runnable rather than ambiguous.
